newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House opens debate on Gingrich punishment. [CORRECTED 20:54 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. House opens debate on Gingrich punishment. [CORRECTED 20:54 GMT]

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives on Tuesday opened debate on a tough proposed ethics punishment for Newt Gingrich following two years of partisan bickering over the controversial House speaker.

"The penalty is tough and unprecedented. It is also appropriate," said Representative Nancy Johnson, chairwoman of the House committee that has recommended a reprimand and a $300,000 "fine" for Gingrich as penalty for admitted ethics breaches.
"No one is above the rules of the House of Represenatives," she said.

The 435-member House is expected to approve the penalty later on Tuesday. Gingrich, who was re-elected speaker just two weeks ago, would be the first sitting speaker ever to be reprimanded. The speaker is the third highest elected official of the United States after the president and vice president.

The proposed punishment was for bringing discredit on the House by giving false statements to the ethics committee and for failing to seek legal advice on use of tax-free charitable contributions for partisan political purposes.
The ethics committee said the offence called for a penalty "somewhere in between" a reprimand and the more serious censure, which would have almost certainly required Gingrich to step down.
Recent opinion polls have suggested Gingrich is one of the most unpopular politicians in the United States, with only about a third of Americans approving of the job he is doing.
Gingrich appeared before House Republicans in a closed party caucus on Tuesday morning before the vote.
Some Republicans emerging from the meeting voiced concern at the monetary penalty. Representative Bill McCollum of Florida, told reporters, "This $300,000 is wrong. Any amount of money is wrong."

Republican Sherwood Boehlert of New York, said the penalty set a dangerous precedent. "Any one of us could be charged with some kind of inadvertent act... it really sets a very dangerous precedent," he said.

Representative David McIntosh of Indiana said the size of the penalty "surprised everyone" and had sparked discussion of a "loser pays" proposal under which members filing complaints that were dismissed would pay towards the cost of the investigation.

The Gingrich ethics case has been the subject of fierce political jockeying. But as the vote approached both Republicans and Democrats said they wanted to get the vote on his punishment behind them and return to working on issues such as a balanced budget and social programmes.
One of the major themes of President Bill Clinton's inaugural address on Monday was a call for bipartisan cooperation between the Republican-controlled Congress and the Democratic White House.

Speaking on NBC's "Today" show early on Tuesday, Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, said one of the reasons for the committee's verdict "is to try to put this era of animosity and divisiveness and partisanship behind the House."
